title: Bài sưu tầm 219 - Passage 2: Secrets of the Annual Ring: Dendroclimatology and Volcanic Cataclysms
passageHtml:
READING PASSAGE 219

Secrets of the Annual Ring: Dendroclimatology and Volcanic Cataclysms

Paragraph A. To the casual observer, a cross-section of a felled tree presents a simple sequence of concentric wooden rings, recording the passage of biological years. To paleoclimatologists, however, these rings represent high-fidelity climatic archives of exquisite precision. The science of dendroclimatology operates on a straightforward biological principle: in temperate and sub-polar zones where growth is halted by winter dormancy, trees produce exactly one distinct ring of wood per year. The width and cellular density of each annual ring are determined by the environmental conditions experienced during the spring and summer growing season. When temperatures are warm and rainfall is plentiful, trees produce broad, robust rings; when conditions are cold or dry, growth stalls, leaving behind microscopic, narrow bands.

Paragraph B. By overlapping the ring patterns of living ancient trees with preserved timbers excavated from historic buildings, bogs, and archaeological ruins, researchers have assembled continuous unbroken master tree-ring chronologies extending back over ten thousand years. The true diagnostic power of this chronology, however, lies in its capacity to pinpoint sudden, anomalous global weather crises. Scattered across thousands of normal rings are rare, catastrophic cellular anomalies known as 'frost rings'. In these bands, plant cells are found structurally crushed, deformed, and frozen midway through their summer division cycle. A frost ring indicates an extreme meteorological event: an unseasonal, sub-zero freeze striking in the dead of midsummer, instantly freezing the living sapwood of trees across entire continents.

Paragraph C. For decades, historians were baffled by contemporary sixth-century chronicles describing a terrifying atmospheric veil that descended over Europe, the Mediterranean, and Asia in 536 CE. The Byzantine historian Procopius wrote that 'the sun gave forth its light without brightness, like the moon, during the whole year.' Crops failed across Ireland, China reported summer snows that starved millions, and widespread societal collapse followed. By analyzing high-altitude bristlecone pines in California and Siberian larches, dendrochronologist Dr. Michael Baillie proved that 536 CE coincided with the most catastrophic growth collapse in two millennia. The tree rings revealed a catastrophic decadal cold shock now known as the Late Antique Little Ice Age.

Paragraph D. The physical cause of these historical tree-ring collapses was long debated, but paleoclimatologists have finally tied them directly to volcanic megathrust eruptions. When a colossal volcano erupts with explosive volcanic explosivity (VEI 6 or higher), it blasts millions of tonnes of sulfur dioxide gas high into the stratosphere, far above the cleansing influence of weather clouds. In the dry stratosphere, the sulfur dioxide reacts chemically with water vapour to create microscopic sulfuric acid aerosols. These reflective sulfate veils encircle the planet within weeks, scattering incoming solar radiation back into space. The resulting volcanic winter can depress global surface temperatures by up to three degrees Celsius for several years, severely shortening agricultural growing seasons and leaving unmistakable cellular scars within the annual wood of trees worldwide.

Paragraph E. To cross-reference tree-ring anomalies with volcanic events, researchers turn to another natural archive: polar ice cores extracted from Greenland and Antarctica. When volcanic aerosol veils eventually settle out of the stratosphere over several years, they precipitate onto polar glaciers, leaving behind distinct layers of acidic sulfate fallout preserved within the annual ice layers. By matching the exact calendar dates of tree-ring frost rings with synchronized sulfate spikes discovered in polar ice cores, paleoclimatologists can determine not only the exact year an ancient volcano erupted, but whether it was located in the Northern Hemisphere, Southern Hemisphere, or equatorial tropics.

Paragraph F. However, reading ancient wood requires sophisticated analytical correction. Dr. Valerie Trouet, a leading dendroclimatologist, emphasizes that not all tree species respond uniformly to environmental shocks. 'Different species possess unique biological sensitivities,' Trouet explains. 'Trees growing near the alpine treeline on high mountains are constrained primarily by summer temperature, making them superb thermometers. Conversely, trees growing in arid lowlands are constrained by moisture, making them sensitive barometers of drought. If an investigator fails to isolate these distinct ecological drivers, they risk misinterpreting a drought signal as an extreme temperature crash.'

Paragraph G. Today, the study of ancient tree rings is playing an indispensable role in contemporary climate debates. By providing an uncorrupted, pre-industrial record of global climate variability spanning millennia, dendroclimatology establishes the baseline against which modern anthropogenic warming must be evaluated. The rings prove that while natural volcanic eruptions trigger sudden, dramatic cold snaps, the sustained, planetary warming observed over the past fifty years is wholly unprecedented in both speed and geographic extent across the entire Holocene epoch. Ancient wood, it turns out, holds the baseline truths necessary to understand our perilous climatic future.

groups.title: Questions 19–20
groups.instructions:
Choose TWO letters, A–E.
Write the correct letters in boxes 19 and 20 on your answer sheet.
Which TWO facts about dendroclimatology are mentioned by the writer in the text?
options: A. Trees located in desert regions provide the most accurate measurements of historical temperature.
B. Ancient master tree-ring records have been constructed extending back more than ten millennia.
C. Tropical trees produce more distinct annual rings than trees growing in sub-polar climates.
D. The width of an annual tree ring reflects the weather conditions present during its growth period.
E. Modern global warming is very similar in speed to natural temperature cycles in pre-industrial history.
